title: Abnormal Liver Tests, Normal Abdomen / Say Normal, Invent Nothing, Then Plan the Work-Up

blocks.text: Abnormal Liver Tests, Normal Abdomen / Say Normal, Invent Nothing, Then Plan the Work-Up

AMaC MRCP PACES · R2-12 · Physical examination · PACES Station 4, abdominal examination encounter · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 min: up to 6 min examining, then at least 4 min of examiner questions · Guidelines: BSG guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests (Newsome et al, Gut 2018;67:6-19) · Related AMaC: Abdominal examination: chronic liver disease; splenomegaly

A 47-year-old woman, a catering supervisor, was found to have abnormal liver blood tests at a health check. She feels well. Please examine her abdomen and report what you find. You have up to 6 minutes to examine, followed by questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A normal abdomen does not make abnormal liver tests normal; report the examination as normal without inventing signs, then plan the work-up.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates expect signs and invent a liver edge, a spider naevus or a spleen tip to fit the story. Pass: examine fully, report normal findings plainly, then plan the work-up. Fail: report a sign that is not there.

rows: Examine everything: signs may be absent, not hidden.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. High-performance includes the pass behaviours. This station-specific grid is an AMaC teaching framework mapped to PACES skills, not an official mark scheme. Consent, hand hygiene, dignity and an appropriate chaperone are baseline professional practice.
Not used for this station type: the patient is a real or simulated patient and the findings are in section 8.

Findings (released as each step is done). Normal examination. Hands, eyes and skin normal; no jaundice or spider naevi. Abdomen soft, non-tender; liver and spleen not palpable; no ascites; no masses; hernial orifices intact; bowel sounds normal. No oedema. Pulse 72, BP 124/76 (scenario values). Liver blood tests, only if the candidate asks: ALT 96 U/L, AST 58 U/L, GGT mildly raised, bilirubin, ALP and albumin normal (hepatitic pattern; scenario values).

Question ladder. Q1 Findings (R3): the abdominal examination is normal. Q2 Causes of abnormal liver tests (R4): fatty liver, alcohol, medicines and supplements, viral hepatitis, autoimmune, iron overload, biliary disease. Q3 First-line work-up (R5): bilirubin, albumin, ALT, ALP, GGT, full blood count; ultrasound; hepatitis B and C serology, autoimmune markers, immunoglobulins, ferritin and transferrin saturation (BSG 2018). Q4 Referral (R6): urgent if unexplained jaundice, suspected cancer, marked derangement or synthetic failure.
Normal-findings variant. This station is the normal variant. If a candidate finds a sign, the examiner says nothing is found.
Curveball 1. "Is she healthy?" Safe: a normal examination does not exclude liver disease; the tests need working up.
Curveball 2. "She has yellow eyes." Safe: jaundice needs urgent assessment.
Curveball 3. "Should we repeat the same tests in a month?" Safe: repeating the same panel alone is not recommended.

Fail performance
(Presses into the abdomen and does not ask about pain. [R1 Fail] Palpates only. [R2 Fail])
CANDIDATE: I can feel the liver edge and a spider naevus. [R3 Fail] It is fatty liver. [R4 Fail]
EXAMINER: What would you do?
CANDIDATE: Repeat the liver tests. [R5 Fail] She can go home. [R6 Fail]
Examiner note: No consent, signs invented, one cause and no work-up or safety net.

(Looks at hands, eyes and neck, inspects, palpates, percusses and checks for ascites. [R2 Pass])

CANDIDATE: Thank you. I'll cover you. [R1 Pass]

EXAMINER: What could explain the abnormal tests?
CANDIDATE: Fatty liver, alcohol, drugs, viral, autoimmune, iron and biliary causes; a normal examination does not exclude them. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: How would you investigate?
CANDIDATE: Alcohol and drug history, liver tests, ultrasound, hepatitis B and C serology, autoimmune markers, immunoglobulins, ferritin and transferrin saturation. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: When would you refer?
CANDIDATE: Urgently for jaundice or suspected cancer. If fatty liver is likely I'd assess fibrosis, and I'd tell her to return if she turns yellow. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: Thank you for letting me examine you. [R1 High]
Examiner note: Reported normal findings and set out the work-up and safety net.
R3: Reporting a liver edge or spider naevus that is not there shows signs were invented to fit the story.
R5: Repeating the same panel, or going to biopsy first, skips the recommended first-line work-up.
R4: Naming one cause only narrows the work-up too early.
R6: Reassuring and discharging misses jaundice or cancer that needs urgent referral.
R2: Palpating without checking hands, eyes and ascites means a normal result is not credible.
"I haven't found any abnormal signs."
"A normal examination does not exclude liver disease."
"I'd start with the history and the first-line tests."
Say normal when it is normal; do not invent signs.

BSG 2018: first-line liver tests are bilirubin, albumin, ALT, ALP and GGT, with a blood count; repeating the panel alone without investigating the cause is usually insufficient, unless a transient insult is strongly suspected.
Adult aetiology screen: ultrasound, hepatitis B and C serology, autoimmune markers, immunoglobulins, ferritin with transferrin saturation.
Refer urgently for unexplained jaundice, suspected hepatic or biliary cancer, marked derangement or synthetic failure.

Aetiological assessment should accompany repeat testing when indicated. Review alcohol, prescribed and non-prescribed medicines, viral risks and metabolic risks; assess the biochemical pattern and synthetic function. A standard adult screen includes ultrasound, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody with confirmatory testing if positive, autoimmune markers, immunoglobulins, ferritin and transferrin saturation.
THINK: Jaundice or cancer; silent liver disease.
SAY: "The abdominal examination is normal."
DO: Consent; hands and eyes; liver, spleen, ascites.
NUMBERS: Pulse 72, BP 124/76 (scenario values).
TRAP: Inventing a sign.
FINISH: Alcohol and drug history; first-line tests; ultrasound; BSG screen.

BSG guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests (Newsome et al, Gut 2018;67:6-19). Recommendations 1 to 5; standard liver aetiology screen. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5754852/.
